profile.campus: Texas Research Park, Bexar County, Texas (Microsoft San Antonio data center campus)
profile.reading:
This building sits in Microsoft's Texas Research Park data center campus in Bexar County, on a street named for a Greek letter (Lambda Drive or Omicron Drive), a naming pattern Microsoft has used across several San Antonio-area buildings identified by press as SAT40 and related facilities. The San Antonio Report, drawing on public filings, reported Microsoft paid roughly $175.9 million to develop the SAT40 building on about 70 acres in Texas Research Park, part of a broader San Antonio-region footprint that had grown to at least eight Microsoft data centers by August 2023, with cumulative investment across Bexar and Medina counties exceeding $1.2 billion since Microsoft first opened two San Antonio facilities in 2015 at roughly $90 million each. San Antonio's city council approved a 15-year Chapter 380 tax reimbursement in 2013 covering 40% of property taxes in exchange for a $250 million Microsoft investment commitment and the creation of 20 high-paying jobs, an incentive structure local reporting has scrutinized given how many subsequent Microsoft expansions the city has continued to subsidize. Construction phases at Microsoft's San Antonio campuses have typically employed several hundred workers, while each completed data center building tends to run with a comparatively small operating staff of roughly 50 employees once online; San Antonio's broader data processing and hosting sector employed 5,066 people at average annual earnings of about $96,906 as of the most recent figures cited. Microsoft has not published this specific building's square footage or MW capacity, consistent with its general practice of disclosing detailed specs for named projects like SAT40 or SAT14 but not for every individual structure on a shared campus.

CPS Energy, San Antonio's municipally owned electric and gas utility, the largest such public utility in the country, supplies power to Microsoft's San Antonio-area campuses and has cited large commercial and industrial customers, data centers among them, in its own integrated resource planning as it weighs new generation to meet growing demand. Because CPS Energy is municipally owned rather than investor-owned, large-load agreements with customers like Microsoft are negotiated directly with the city-owned utility rather than through the Public Utility Commission of Texas process that governs most of the state's investor-owned utilities.

reading.body:
This building is part of Microsoft's Texas Research Park campus in Bexar County, one of at least eight Microsoft data centers the company has built in the San Antonio region since 2015 with cumulative investment exceeding $1.2 billion. Microsoft has not published this facility's power capacity or square footage, consistent with its practice of disclosing specs for named projects like SAT40 but withholding details for individual structures on shared campuses. The campus sits within a broader Texas footprint where 133 facilities are mapped but only 18 have published power figures, leaving this site's scale relative to the state's AI infrastructure unclear from available data.

Power to Microsoft's San Antonio campuses comes from CPS Energy, the country's largest municipally owned electric and gas utility, which has explicitly identified data centers as part of its load planning for new generation capacity. Because CPS Energy is city-owned rather than regulated by the Public Utility Commission of Texas, power agreements with Microsoft are negotiated directly between the utility and the company rather than through the state's standard utility oversight process. The utility's need to plan generation around large data center loads suggests this campus is material to San Antonio's grid, though CPS Energy's available capacity and any constraints it faces are not published.

San Antonio's city council approved a 15-year tax reimbursement covering 40 percent of property taxes in 2013 to secure Microsoft's initial investment commitment, a subsidy structure the local press has noted has continued through subsequent expansions without published updates to the underlying investment or job commitments. Operating employment at completed data center buildings tends to be small, roughly 50 employees per facility once online, while construction phases employ several hundred workers temporarily. Without published power or capacity for this specific campus, its significance to AI scaling depends on what Microsoft has built into the broader San Antonio footprint, a figure the company has not disclosed.
